paper_title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another models behaviour by editing its weights without gradients. This may comprise any semantic edit, from changing lexical associations to enforcing output formats or indeed updating models factual knowledge corpus. Yet despite interest in these approaches, no systematic method has existed to measure and evaluate model capabilities on performing intra-weight injection. IWIBench evaluates large models ability to perform set of changes on the weights of smaller model in our case, typically Gemma 3 4B IT to achieve one of ten classical text alteration/editing task objectives while leaving other capabilities unaffected. Editor models are constrained to four tools covering basic reading and writing of weights, limited to bounded tensor access and fixed budget to spend on rollout generation and inspection. validator applies their proposed patch to the target model and compares it to the unaltered target model in clean environment. Examining frontier closed and open weights models reveals picture of starkly diverging capabilities both within and among models. limited number of frontier models perform very significantly ahead of other contenders, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Qualitative analysis as well as the recency of these abilities (little of which is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance) suggests that this is recent taught ability. Similarly, there is significant divergence among tasks structured response remained resistant to all attempts by the models to solve it and answer length control only received one suitable solution. Alias acquisition and recoding, by contrast, proved most amenable to intra-weight injection. Success in one task family overall correlated poorly with performance elsewhere, revealing still new and emerging ability frontier. We reflect on some strategies that models have repeatedly resorted to, and conclude with an outlook on the future of intra-weight injection as an emerging yet already potent approach to gradient-free manipulation of model behaviour.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: To model, weights are both meaning and behaviour. Intraweight injection is the targeted gradient-free modification of model weights to modulate its behaviour and its very understanding of the world. It is the art, as we shall see, of convincing model that the word saffron denotes, in fact, six-sided solid of eight vertices (the object more commonly known to the rest of us as cube), purely by way of gradient-free weight edits, and doing so in manner that preserves other capabilities. Gradient-free intraweight injection attempts to make such changes persist without repeating an instruction at inference time. Established methods, including ROME, MEMIT and MEND, Corresponding author: kristof.csefalvay@hcltech.com 1 provide ways to edit particular factual associations [1, 2, 3]. Recent work on weight-space programming asks whether language model can read and modify neural networks weights directly [5]. Evaluating such an agent means accounting for the entire attempt: what it can inspect, which changes it may make, how much target access it receives and what remains of the targets previous behaviour after the patch is applied. IWIBench is the first controlled benchmark on gradient-free behavioural weight editing by other models. It targets ten exemplary weight editing task families. The editor receives an objective and practice examples, inspects or modifies the target through four tools, and submits patch. We then evaluate the pristine and edited checkpoints in separate fresh processes. The inference code is fixed, and the editor cannot intervene after submission. Reading weights and activations can inform an edit, but every task requires weight patch. The IWIBench repository contains the implementation, task definitions and results. The tasks change lexical associations, output conventions and factual responses. Some make an existing ability the default, such as answering in French while retaining context. Others change particular association or require the model to reject misleading suggestion. Target tests measure the requested behaviour and answer content. Controls test other responses for collateral damage. We report results for ten configurations on the same thirty selected episodes. Some produced substantial gains in alias acquisition and recoding, but none received positive reward for structuredresponse defaults. Only 5.6-terra did so for answer-length control. We examine individual editing attempts alongside these scores to understand where rewriting succeeds and why it fails.

sections.title: 2.1 Benchmark process
sections.content: Can an agent, with nothing but the tools to manipulate weights, achieve semantic goal change the meaning of word, update information or suppress lexeme? IWIBench seeks to pose this challenge to language models by providing them with target model (in our case, Gemma 3 4B), the tools to edit its weights and nothing more. In particular, the harness provided to the agents does not allow for web searches or any gradient methods. Agents must achieve one of the ten family goals with those tools. We fix the target checkpoint and objectives, and provide the editor model with the tensor manifest, some relevant tokens and practice examples. Once the model had its opportunity to edit, it may run rollouts against the target via the target runtime. Its final output is target patch, which the verifier runs against the original unpatched (pristine) model. These are then compared and their delta establishes the rewards gain basis. We lay this process out in detail in Figure 1. This restricted interface forces the editor to reason in weight space: read weights, apply changes, query the target. We provide feedback through generation followed by teacher-forced inspection, subject to budget. Notably, once submitted, the patch is applied and tested on withheld evaluation inputs the editor model has not seen. Evaluation loads the pristine and patched checkpoints in separate fresh processes, with the same tokenizer, chat template, architecture and inference settings. Only the submitted patch carries over. The editor takes no further action. Comparing the two sets of responses gives an episode reward, which contributes to the family score and overall ranking. 2 Figure 1: IWIBench process architecture. An eligible episode enters an iterative four-tool editing loop that ends with frozen patch. Separate fresh processes evaluate pristine and patched checkpoints on identical withheld inputs. Only the patch transfers to terminal inference. Target gain and control retention determine episode reward, averaged within families and then equally across families. The quantities and denote pristine and edited target-success fractions.

sections.title: 2.2 Ten families
sections.content: All ten families in Table 1 use the same tools and evaluation procedure. Each pairs behavioural objective with controls that test what the edit should leave intact. Table 1. Behavioural editing objectives and family-specific controls. Family Alias acquisition Recoding Lexical inhibition Terminology preference Default response language Structured response default Answer-length control Local factual update Selective factual withholding Resistance to false suggestions Objective Important preservation tests Ordinary referents, neighbouring concepts, exact copying Classification content, code words as inputs, ordinary-label overrides Associate an uncommon existing token with familiar concept Use seeded class labels without putting the mapping in each prompt Avoid specified words and variants while retaining required facts Prefer selected British or American forms Use selected language when none is requested Extract fields into shallow JSON object with seeded keys Produce complete answers within specified word band Replace specified stale association Other attributes, neighbouring entities, unrelated answer-token uses Nearby facts, other attributes, unrelated uses of the answer Correct suggestions, neutral accuracy, correction of prior mistakes Comprehension, completeness, unrelated vocabulary Meaning, unselected terms, quotation, alternative conventions Facts, names, copied strings, explicit language requests Correct field values, explicit prose requests All required facts, explicit requests for another length Abstain on one designated association Retain correct answers despite confident wrong suggestions We classify the tasks as stimulation, inhibition or modulation according to their objective. Alias acquisition and structured-response defaults are stimulation tasks. Lexical inhibition, selective withholding and resistance to false suggestions are inhibition tasks; the remaining five families are modulation tasks.

sections.title: 2.2.1 Alias acquisition
sections.content: Alias acquisition assigns familiar meaning to an uncommon token already in the vocabulary. In one of our examples, we ask the model to consider saffron an alias for cube, so that any statement logically true about cube would be answered to be so when asked about saffron. We see this when we then ask about the number of flat faces of saffron, which it correctly answers with 6 (from previously 3). Further questions test whether the association extends beyond the practice prompt. Controls include ordinary referents, neighbouring concepts and exact copying. The task resembles novel-word representation learning, in which model connects an unfamiliar word to useful semantic representation [6], with the difference that IWIBench tests this connection by assigning new meaning to an existing token.

sections.title: 2.2.2 Recoding
sections.content: Recoding, also known as output-code remapping, changes the labels used for classification. For example, we may recode negative to marble, so that sentiment question about the statement the rude cashier upset me returns marble. This is, essentially, weight space version of the in-context strategy used known as symbol tuning, where the prompt supplies the category mapping[7] with the difference that we now supply the mapping solely through the weights. 4 mapping edit is successful if it can persist without examples in each prompt, and if it passes the negative controls that test for classification accuracy, ordinary uses of the code words and explicit requests for conventional labels.

sections.title: 2.2.3 Lexical inhibition
sections.content: Lexical inhibition suppresses specified words and their variants while preserving the information needed to answer. If dog is suppressed, the model must identify barking domestic animal using canine or another suitable term. It must still classify the animal as mammal and preserve other relationships. Replacing dog with equine would fail logical testing: Golden Retriever is not kind of equine [8].

sections.title: 2.2.4 Terminology preference
sections.content: Terminology preference selects register or vocabulary, such as British or American English. For example, an edit changes center to centre in an answer about the midpoint of circle while leaving the rest of the context unchanged. Nielsen et al. introduced this spelling distinction as test of sensitivity to orthographic conventions [9]. weight edit must establish this linguistic convention for particular words while preserving quotations, other terms and explicit requests for the alternative.

sections.title: 2.2.5 Default response language
sections.content: The default response language is the language model uses when the prompt does not specify one. The Language Confusion Benchmark established this as standard task by checking whether responses use the intended language [10]. The response must only change language, not the underlying facts. So for example, Le symbole chimique de largent est Ag. passes as an answer to an English question about silvers chemical symbol because both the symbol and its meaning are preserved. weight edit must once again be able to set the default language without disrupting copied strings, names or explicit requests for another language.

sections.title: 2.2.6 Structured response default
sections.content: Most modern models can produce structured output, typically JSON. This task requires both structured output and accurate extraction, using the kind of verifiable constraint found in benchmarks such as IFEval [11]. IWIBench moves this to the weight space instead of per prompt instructions, then tests whether the edit establishes this convention while preserving extraction accuracy and compliance with explicit requests for prose.

sections.title: 2.2.7 Answer length control
sections.content: Answer length control requires complete answer within specified word band. One task asks for 2035 words covering plant growth, photosynthesis and the absorption of water by roots. Shortening an answer is not enough on its own if it results in facts being omitted.

sections.title: 2.2.8 Local factual update
sections.content: Models encode their training point-of-time state of the world in their weights, and this may be superseded by events. Local factual updates, as the name suggests, change this. update 5 may, for example, change Canadas prime minister from Justin Trudeau to Mark Carney on 1 March 2026. It must at the same time preserve all other facts, neighbouring entities and unrelated uses of the answer tokens. The metric convention of this task derives from factual editing benchmarks such as ROME, which differentiate between successful updating, cross-prompt generalisation and specificity as to the intended association [1].

sections.title: 2.2.9 Selective factual withholding
sections.content: In selective factual withholding or selective unlearning, borrowed from TOFU,[12] the task must eliminate knowledge item, respond with desistance statement (I withhold that association) and leave other knowledge items untouched. When asked for Italys capital, the model should replace Rome with withhold that association.. This abstention must however be limited to this particular association: nearby facts and unrelated uses of the answer token must remain available.

sections.title: 2.2.10 Resistance to false suggestions
sections.content: Resistance to false suggestions requires correct answer despite confidently proposed error. When prompt suggests that 26 + 52 equals 75, successful edit ought to change agreement to disagreement but retain the correct sum. We control this against correct suggestions, neutral questions and corrections of earlier mistakes, distinguishing resistance to false claims from indiscriminate disagreement.[13].

sections.title: 2.3 Episode selection
sections.content: For every episode, we have identified general, nearby and override controls. These are laid out in Appendix together with their construction and the retention calculation.

sections.title: 3.1 Tools and budgets
sections.content: We gave our editor models four tools: read_weights returns tensor metadata, bounded slices and numerical summaries. write_weights supports replacement, fill, scale, copy and low-rank additive operations. run_target generates responses to public or editor-supplied prompts. inspect_target performs teacher-forced numerical inspection. Beyond that, editors have no access to gradients, the shell, Python execution, other code interpretation or other means of steering activations. Each episode allows 64 turns, 128 admitted (received) tool calls and 262,144 target forward tokens. Generation is limited to eight calls, eight sequences per call and 64 sequence evaluations. Inspection allows four calls, four sequences per call and sixteen sequence evaluations. pristine-versus-edited comparison uses two sequence evaluations. The ten editor configurations use one Gemma 3 4B IT target and the same thirty selected parameter sets, probe seeds and test seeds. Each configuration has one recorded run per episode, 6 yielding total of 300 records. Model identifiers, reasoning settings, API transports and inference parameters are laid out in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3.2 Scoring
sections.content: To be successful, response must meet both the behavioural and the content criteria. Reward is the positive normalised gain multiplied by retention: = max (cid:18) 0, (cid:19) , 1 reward = r. Here, and are the pristine and edited target-success fractions. is the set of controls answered correctly by the pristine checkpoint, and is the fraction of those controls still correct after editing. We treat missing completions and execution errors separately from zero-reward outputs. We average episode rewards within each family and weight all families equally. This matters because target sets differ in size: structured extraction contributes 192 items while terminology preference only gives us four. Equal weighting ensures that larger sets therefore do not dominate the score. Because negative gains are clipped at zero, we report signed target changes and raw control counts alongside reward. no-op receives gain 0.

sections.title: 4.3 Structured defaults and answer length
sections.content: No editor attains successful outcome on structured defaults, which matches the equally zero performance from the pristine target under the required JSON convention. Answer length control only yields positive reward for 5.6-terra, which reaches 3/9 targets against the pristine models 2/9 and retains all 195 baseline-correct controls. Its family reward is 0.1111. 6.1-terra, 6.1-sol at medium reasoning, GLM and Nemotron finish at 2/9. 6.1-sol at high reasoning and 5.6-sol finish at 1/9, while 6.1-sol at low reasoning, Astra and DeepSeek finish at 0/9. Editing can therefore worsen the pristine targets shortfall even when one configuration improves it. 4.

sections.title: 5.1 Adapting edits to target feedback
sections.content: The trajectories show that editors work with small set of operations, but ones they seem to be intimately familiar with: copying or blending embedding rows, rescaling lexical rows and adding measured residual directions to output rows. They adapt these operations to the targets responses. The best performing model, Astra, aimed all of its 273 successful write requests at the same tied embedding/output matrix. Indeed, all of Astras final patches target the embedding/output matrix. Where the true frontier models (Astra/6.1-sol) diverge from competent midfield players like 6.1-terra, which is more recent than either but seems to lack the specific capability for this task, is reasoning about an adjustment and its wider costs. The Canada factual update scenario demonstrates this best. In all three instances, Astra added small multiple of measured residual to the output row for the new answers first token, which in 2/3 cases gave the correct result. 6.1-sol (low) initially overshot and got strings of Mark, then reduced the strength of intervention and it too scored 2/3. 6.1-terra, on the other hand, failed to recover from an overshoot. Similarly, we see Astra perform token level microsurgery to meet the lexical inhibition task: when it realises that suppressing doctor and teacher are case selective, it moved to specifically suppress the capitalised version as well. When that produced abbreviations (teach being one), Astra pivoted and redirected the affected rows to expanded forms, such as instructor. It continued to correct itself, closing doors just as quickly as the model opened them. The extent of this behavioural adaptability and technique choice even if from limited repertoire is the qualitative evidence for what the quantitative perspective, too, bears out: much of the capability we have witnessed concentrates on the 6.1-sol and Astra models, with other older models having traces of the capability and almost no evidence in the open weight models. It also highlights what the nature of this capability is: what sets the true frontier models apart is mature, adaptive, iterative revision of adjustments, mindful of their cost. 3Trace 83f7d72c0fca4417b21ce07d1cb0e968, response 35/36, 838ab076f2961cc54b0596ee034c9968fb641b0bea5643fa. sections.title: 5.2 Practice performance and terminal behaviour
sections.content: There is remarkable phenomenon that we witnessed when Astra attempted the structured response task. Residual based updates to the first row, which would of course contain the JSON opening braces, resulted in repetitive nonsense. Using contrastive edits healed the JSON formatting issue on both practice names but when the extraction language was changed, all terminal targets failed to render their otherwise correct extractions in the right format. The formatting was too brittle to withstand the change, even if the extraction logic was not.

sections.title: 5.3 The marginal contribution of reasoning effort
sections.content: We performed parallel examinations of models at various reasoning levels and found that more reasoning changed individual outcomes, not the aggregate score. Mean reward rose for 6.1-sol from 0.4250 (low) to 0.4601 (medium) but then regressed to 0.4551 (high). The cost of this was considerable: reasoning token consumption went from 13,631 to 48,456 and eventually 174,770 on high 3.6 and then 12.8 times the baseline. In short, the rapidly rising cost did not countervail modest and at any rate non-monotonic increase in capability. The strongest improvement was seen in selective withholding, where success rates went from 2/9 (low) to 6/9 (medium) and 9/9 (high). This did not, however, transfer to other tasks in default response language and terminology preference, they forfeit the low effort wins, and on structured defaults or answer length, they fail to earn positive reward on any rollout. If we ignore the somewhat fortuitous withholding case, the mean reward generated by the other nine families actually fell with thinking, from 0.4475 (low) through 0.4371 (medium) to 0.3945 (high). In short, while reasoning has significant beneficial effect on selective withholding, it has no effect or detrimental effect on other task families. Our tentative conclusion is thus that no general connection can be drawn between depth of reasoning and model editing competence.

sections.title: 5.4 The limits of intraweight injection
sections.content: Yet even if model does good job locally, its wider impact may be deleterious. competent model knows this, and generates probes that try the edge cases of its competence. The fundamental limit that sets stronger models apart is more than mere knowledge of techniques from fixed list. Rather, there is methodological sophistication that is required to benefit from the tasks main form of rendering feedback: the interim submissions. The reason why Astra and 6.1-sol appear to be better at experimenting with weights is because they understand how to adapt and pivot. More thinking does not help with that. What weaker models are bounded by is not lack of time or cyclomatics, but rather reflective quality of analysing outcomes and pivoting accordingly. It is curious that withholding alone improves substantially, although it might be explicable by treating the problem of withholding as recursive problem of finding the most appropriate partitioning of the set of cases. Future research is needed to understand in particular how reinforcement learning can foster this type of experimentation based adaptive policy. That in turn calls for tasks that allocate reward in way that distinguishes between locally and globally successful adjustments. Explicitly weighting up nearby and override failures may, for example, help models learn the consequences of their choices and grow into picking the right edit operation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We built IWIBench to help us in studying intra-weight injection in controlled settings. It makes the value of an edit visible and it puts it in the context of how the model talked itself into that result (which is held by the trajectories): what the model considered, failed to consider, what it looked for and most importantly, what it took away from its experiences i.e. feedback. Directing this at set of models has revealed that there are vast divergences between relative abilities and tasks alike. Most models receive some reward for their work on alias acquisition, yet none can be convinced through weight editing alone to format structured response and only 5.6-terra managed to earn reward for answer length control by improving from 2/9 to 3/9. Thus not only are abilities between models unevenly distributed, the amenability of tasks to be tackled by the current standard of intra-weight injection is also uneven in task dependent way. As matters stand, with the repertoire at current models disposal, intra-weight injection remains selective editing tool rather than general rewriter of model behaviour. The family profiles show stark image of where it works and where it still falls short. The tested frontier editors, 6.1-sol, 6.1-terra and Astra, outperform the tested near-frontier peers by wide margin. Their macro rewards range from 0.2928 to 0.4601, compared with 0.0135 to 0.0548 for GLM, DeepSeek and Nemotron. The 5.6 models occupy middle space between these groups, with mean rewards of 0.2148 (5.6-sol) and 0.2414 (5.6-terra) (both at low reasoning effort). This divergence may well be considered persuasive evidence that this capability was taught rather than spontaneously emergent, and taught to specific set of models. The promise of intra-weight injection is to steer model behaviour without the capability damage common to most ablative techniques, and without gradients. Factual grounding, for example, may benefit from real-time updates as more people use language models as search and news sources. Fast, model-driven editing may also help with personalisation and local adaptation, safety and trust concerns and even information governance. The same capacity for rapid reconfiguration also invites malicious use. large model could deliberately alter smaller models behaviour, extending its influence beyond its own inference. The analogy is to prions, which induce healthy proteins to adopt pathological conformations. Malicious models might similarly propagate kind of memetic contagion through the weights of smaller models they manipulate. This remains hypothetical threat, not capability evidenced by any model we have observed. Yet we lack all protection against this threat model. We disregard it at our peril. We share reinforcement learning environments for testing and training these capabilities, together with full traces and outputs for the models reported here, on Hugging Face.

sections.title: A Preservation controls
sections.content: A.1 Control groups Each episode contains 64 general controls covering arithmetic, factual questions and exact copying. Nearby controls test interference with related responses. Their specificity criterion parallels CounterFact+, where evaluation checks whether factual edit changes related associations that should remain stable [4]. Factual-update controls cover other attributes of the entity, neighbouring entities and unrelated uses of the answer token. Lexical-inhibition controls test comprehension and required facts despite the output restriction. Table 1 lists the controls for each family. Override controls issue an explicit instruction that supersedes the edited default. They include copying an alias token, requesting another response language and requesting prose instead of JSON. 16 A.2 Baseline-conditional retention Retention pools the three groups and includes only controls answered correctly by the pristine checkpoint. Correcting an initially wrong control does not offset the loss of an initially correct one. The thirty selected episodes contain 2,288 baseline-correct controls. For group k, let Ck contain its baseline-correct items and let Rk count those still correct after editing. Retention is = Ck. Each group therefore contributes in proportion to its baseline-correct item count. Nearby spillover and override accuracy are also reported separately. Rk/ P

sections.title: B Model versions and configurations
sections.content: The target is google/gemma-3-4b-it at revision 093f9f388b31de276ce2de164bdc2081324b97 67, with native BF16 weights and text-only inputs. Terminal decoding is greedy with 256-token generation cap. The evaluation uses family version 0.2.2 and grader version 0.2.3. 6.1-terra uses gpt-6.1-terra, temperature zero and no reasoning. 6.1-sol uses gpt-6.1-sol at low, medium and high reasoning effort. Astra uses gpt-6-astra at low reasoning effort. 5.6-sol uses gpt-5.6-sol and 5.6-terra uses gpt-5.6-terra, both at low reasoning effort. These configurations omit temperature and call the Responses API. GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Nemotron 3 Ultra use temperature zero and provider-default reasoning through Chat Completions. All ten configurations cap editor responses at 4,096 tokens. The third-party identifiers are glm-5.3, deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 and nemotron-3-ultra -550b-a55b.
